items.title: Three slips in the diverticulosis paragraph
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P4
items.my_version: This is likely caused by diverticulosis, a disease that causes herniated pockets to form in the intestines which aren't supported by smooth muscle. There's no known cure for this disease, except possibly glutamine, based on one incomplete clinical trial, which found 2 of 9 women had incredible reductions in diverticula. Glutamine is an amino acid that's the fuel for small intestinal cells, so this makes some sense. 10% of people get side effects from it (including constipation). Butyrate is the fuel for the colon cells. I would also suggest diosmin for improving blood vessel integrity.

items.title: What the gut "cements"
items.where: the opening, P4
items.my_version: Keep in mind that gut health is intimately linked to mental health, as the gut is considered our "second brain." Some people think their guts are working fine, but they notice other health problems, including mental health, and don't realize that all disease begins in the gut, to quote Hippocrates, the founder of Western Medicine. Of course, that's obviously not true, because stress can come from other vectors, but the gut is central to the feedback loop and can cement the stress coming from those other vectors.

items.title: The cells that don't get the energy
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P19
items.my_version: Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine and butyrate). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't get that energy, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.

items.title: What SCFAs do for the barrier
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P23
items.my_version: The colonocytes lining your large intestine are fueled by short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, while your small intestine runs on glutamine. Your gut bacteria make SCFAs when they ferment raw resistant starch, and you get SCFAs directly from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt too. Besides feeding the colonocytes, SCFAs lock down the barrier in your lower gut, so dangerous substances can't escape from gut to blood, and your body can turn down the inflammatory signals it would otherwise need to contain the damage.

items.title: Who needs glutamine
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P24
items.my_version: Some people will tell you to take malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) as an extra quick energy source for your enterocytes. And they do supply quick energy, because they are made and used by that mitochondrial energy cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle. But glutamine is still the main thing your enterocytes need, because it helps build new cells in addition to giving the needed energy. Those acids do help you absorb iron, even two or three times better according to one study where people ate rice with 1g pure malic acid or citric acid mixed in (Gillooly et al., 1983). That's probably because the acids help keep the iron dissolved so the gut can take it up. So something sour with an iron-rich meal is worth having anyway.

items.title: What a herx reaction is
items.where: Phase 1: The Pre-Flight Safety Check, P3
items.my_version: Now let's have a look at your bile function. Do you burp extra (not just like one little burp) after fatty meals? Do your stools float (like it's hard to flush), or look like clay? Then your bile is stagnant (not flowing well), and Hale says if you take antimicrobials now, you'll get a herx reaction: the dying microbes release toxins you can't detoxify. So thin the bile first with Beet Flow (an extract of beet greens) or phosphatidylcholine, before starting on any pathogen killing protocol.

items.title: The serious signs, as a list
items.where: Optional Ready-Made Gut Stacks, P8
items.my_version: Some severe symptoms warrant seeing a doctor rather than considering this DIY approach at the moment. Take it seriously if you notice blood in your stool (if it's blood from upper digestive tract, it could be smelly, black & tarry, not red like from lower GI). Other serious signs to note: losing weight fast, severe pain, a fever or dehydration. And if you're pregnant, some herbs and supplements, like berberine, aren't safe. If your immune system is weak, some probiotics could be risky, since they're live bacteria that need to be kept in check to prevent overgrowth. If you have an IBD flare, cancer or another serious illness, the standard disclaimer applies: work out what to take with your doctor instead of putting a stack together yourself.
